title: An Exercise for Practicing Team Dialogue
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article distinguishes "dialogue," an inquiry-based conversation focused on exploring meaning and feelings, from the advocacy-based discussion that dominates most team interactions. Because teams rarely practice this unfamiliar mode, the author offers a structured exercise: pose an open-ended question with no right answer, cap responses at 90 seconds, and require each responder to immediately ask another team member a question rather than defaulting back to advocacy. A second, faster round with a new question reinforces the habit once the team has warmed up. The piece frames this drill as preparation for tackling higher-stakes dialogue questions that inform team decisions later.
points: Dialogue, exploring meaning and feelings through inquiry, is rare in teams because advocacy-based discussion dominates by default.
The exercise requires a compelling, no-right-answer question and a strict 90-second response cap to force genuine listening.
Each responder must immediately pose a question to another team member rather than defaulting back into advocacy.
A second, faster round reinforces the habit before the team tackles a meatier dialogue question tied to an actual decision.
quotes: Advocacy-based discussions dominate in team interactions. Team members propose ideas, advocate for positions, and try to persuade others to accept their viewpoints.
By first engaging in an inquiry-based conversation, team members learn to explore the depth of feelings and meanings that underlie what people believe.
Second, the leader establishes the ground rule that no one is allowed to hold the floor longer than 90 seconds in this exercise.
After their response, that person must immediately ask another team member a question while staying on topic.
The only unacceptable question is: “Um, what do you think about that question?
